newsitem.title: UK: Newspapers' share of ad spending continues to fall.
newsitem.headline: Newspapers' share of ad spending continues to fall.

text.p: Newspapers' share of advertising spending is falling in the world's top five economies, but growth in emerging markets in Asia-Pacific and Latin America is underpinning the demand for newsprint.

Zenith Media, the media planning and buying unit of advertising and marketing group Cordiant Plc, said on Wednesday its World Press Trends 1997 reported the demand for newspapers was falling in the five largest economies -- the United States, Japan, Germany, France and Britain.
"Newspapers are losing share of their advertising markets, principally to television, while circulations are falling as consumers find alternative ways of filling their time," Zenith said.
"In stark contrast to newspapers in mature economies, titles in emerging markets reap the benfits as rising prosperity brings with it rising readerships."
Newspapers are the preferred advertising medium in emerging markets for high-ticket goods. Zenith said demand for newsprint was forecast to rise in 1997 and prices with it.
The share of advertising expenditure held by newspapers in the top five economies fell to 35.2 percent in 1996 from 38.6 percent in 1989.
However Zenth said the rate of loss for newspapers is expected to decelerate in these nations and forecast they would take a 34.2 percent share in 1999, Zenith said.
"Electronic media, much heralded as the successor to print, have shown few signs of attracting a significant share of marketing spend," Zenith said.

Newspaper expenditure in emerging markets in Asia-Pacific nearly doubled to $9.5 billion in 1996 from $5.6 billion in 1993. But the newspaper share of advertising spending fell to 37.5 percent in 1996 from 39.8 percent in 1993, Zenith said.
Zenith expects newspaper advertsising in emerging Asia-Pacific to rise to $12.9 billion by 1999, accounting for 33.7 percent of the region's total adspend.
Denmark was the heaviest user of newspaper advertising in 1996 at 70 percent, followed by Norway at 61 percent, and Switzerland and Finland at 57 percent each.
